paragraphs.text: The main reason a public speech fails to move it audience is that the speaker has mistakenly believed they are the most important person in the room and then boasts about their achievement. The most successful speakers actually adopt a more humble approach, as Chris Anderson, the curator of the Technology, Entertainment and Design (TED) website, points out. Effective speakers also convince people that they’ve done their research and that what they’re saying matters. In his book TED Talks: The official TED Guide to Public Speaking. Anderson refers to a speech by a business consultant who claimed the main reason a series of businesses had made giant leaps forward is that they had hired his consultancy services. But when prompted, he was reluctant to, or couldn’t, go into detail about the precise thinking behind his methods. Considerably more successful was British education reformer Sir Ken Robinson’s lecture on how schools are killing creativity. He started off by talking about a doctor instead. After he urged her parents to send her to a dance school, she grew up to be a famous choreographer. Robinson’s talk has now been downloaded 35 million times.

Arguably the most important TED Talk to date was given by Anderson himself. Having bought the conference company from its founder, Richard Saul Wurman, he had only 15 minutes when he appeared at the 2002 event to persuade those in attendance that he was the right person to take TED forward. Fortunately for Anderson when he gave his TED Talk, he had done his groundwork beforehand and thoroughly researched his topic, something he regards as a key ingredient of a successful speech. Admitting that he is not a natural speaker, Anderson spoke from the heart, with as much openness and conviction as I could summon. Having just cut his ties with Future Publishing, the British magazine company he had started in 1985 and which at its peak published 150 magazines, Anderson spoke about how ‘TED was a unique place where ideas from all disciplines could be shared.’ Crucially, he won over any doubters in the TED organisation.

The development of online video about, decade ago has proved to be turning point in speech delivery, making people take it a lot more seriously, and recognise the role it plays in global communication. Anderson believes most of un, including children, can benefit from having the ability to talk in front of an audience, ‘certainly think it should be taught in every school because kids now aren’t going to spend their time writing letters to the editor and preparing their written resumes so much as presenting themselves directly on video,’ he says. ‘It’s become more and more important, so people really need to learn how to do this.’ He accepts that public speaking is scary and that everyone is on a spectrum of some level of fear about it, but fees that this can be overcome.

So are there any recommended way to make a memorable speech? Anderson says that although you should rehearse, a degree of flexibility is important in case events suddenly go in an unexpected direction. The issue with some speakers, however, h that they want to memorise their speech word for word. Instead, Anderson says that the content should be so familiar to people that they can just focus on the moment and the audience and what they’re trying to say. He recommends avoiding a formal approach and suggests planning a story about yourself right at the start of the talk so that the audience have a sense of connection with you.

With the length of TED Talks strictly limited to no more than 18 minutes, the ability to arrive quickly at the point you wish to make by remaining concise is vital. After that, you can dedicate whatever’s left over to providing one or two examples for your audience. Despite the potential for a TED Talk to reach millions of people worldwide via the internet, Anderson stresses that speakers must focus on those who are physically present. He advises trying to speak as though you were having a conversation, like you would if you were sitting around with a few friends.

Anderson mentions in his book some extremely popular TED videos that are well worth watching if you want to see what might help you deliver a great speech. In 2007, former US president Bill Clinton gave a talk on the health care system. Humour and warmth, both of which Clinton demonstrated and which his audience found engaging, are valuable speaking devices Back in 200 Canadian novelist Barbara Gowdy simply froze on the TED stage when she learnt that instead of being interviewed in front of the audience, she was expected to speak. The crowd, feeling sympathetic with her situation, began to applaud her. Encouraged by this, she suddenly felt a great rush of energy and began to share her ideas about the writing process So in the end, her nerves actually helped her give the most memorable talk of the conference. And with George Monbiot’s talk, Rewild the World, Anderson encourages people to listen not just to the content, but to how the speaker cleverly makes use of intonation and also a range of gestures. It is impossible, Anderson says, to switch off from the message Monbiot is delivering.
